One of the most grotesque and nauseating self-centred films I’ve seen, protagonists unsympathetic and by the conclusion, not only are the actions bizarre, they are senseless and deplorable with nothing to account for them, the results towards it stilted, their humanity, in terms of emotions and feelings, emptier than whomever they’re blaming, for a film on communication, this one was contrived, lazy and never able to find a purpose in the artificiality, thoughtlessness and even apathy from the protagonists. The dialogue and even actions at the end were creepy and frankly, reeked if a maliciousness the film seems content with, even idealising in its tonality which is confusing as it never seems natural in how it got me in that state. The weirdo who talks about affairs and how it’s nobody’s fault was both interesting in concept and in theory but it seems the notion struggled intensely, when what you have are twisted figures with an internal logic that is as dodgy as that listening to your guts guy, in the sense it seems cute but the movie made it  repugnant in every sense by the end, not one of them can be seen as good or decent, every time just horrible. The funniest bit about this film is that for a film so driven by communication, signals and messages, the four protagonists are the most clueless, the one where she tries to help her fallen husband and tells him to have a good day at work was striking in how tone deaf she was as was the wife of the long haired guy who coincidentally, that very long haired guy was the best at depicting this massively different ways of communicating the most effectively that he comes out the most sympathetic and affable individual though he, like all the rest, has a distance at times but it’s not indifferent or corrosive like our four protagonists, especially that wife who wishes her husband to have a good day at work as one is not that stupid so it has to be pure insidious intent and rancor that is at the heart of her intent.

Four thirty-something friends navigate love, marriage and personal growth while supporting each other through life's challenges. Unlike the previous films I've seen from this director, this film does have a sense of authenticity with characters, and chemistry, that feel genuine. However, the characters themselves are relatively uninteresting and the film fails to highlight anything meaningful about them. It often feels like a series of mundane small moments of their lives played out in real time--like a long workshop in trust exercises or an hour long reading of a dull book. As I'm generally not into slice of life type of stories, this may have been somewhat enjoyable had the characters been more layered or the film been more dynamic but as it is it's dull, lacks spark and is way too long for what little it has. 令人難受。 濱口的去戲劇化並不是為了某種布列松式的極簡主義或是像侯孝賢一般去突出時間的不感症（而其中工作坊一景可能才算得上是碰觸到了這種意圖），相反地，他的電影哲學似乎是在於「能用說的就不要用演的」，也因此煞盡苦心的把所有關於精神的荒漠、性格的碰撞還有道德焦慮都文縐縐的刻進了對白之中。 然而，它劇情的編排卻簡單降智到一個令人驚訝的地步，《歡樂時光》方便的為每個主要角色都設置了一個功能相似的恐慌按鈕以及講述他們如何利用做作的冷漠來逃脫；而事實上，我認為濱口龍介很聰明的把「生活化」的敘事作為這種逃脫的表象，但對於一部長達五個小時的電影而言，這樣的表象顯然遠遠不夠...還有它所呈現（並試圖辯證）的當代生活場景，過於理想化的程度而使其實際上比它想要指責（控訴？）的東西還來的空虛。 而怪異的地方在於，當我終於有辦法靜下來仔細聆聽那些talking heads對某些事情的看法的時候，那些理當可愛的角色卻都顯得如此令人生厭，幾乎是導演帶著惡意可以為之一樣...
317分钟的灾难式观影，核心的中年女性家庭婚姻问题表达太拖沓冗长，对生活的提炼度不够简洁，大量的对话基本上都是枯燥无味的生活上无意义闲谈，过于追求对生活的真实和细枝末节上的全部保留已经脱离了剧情的核心表达，剪这么长简直是多此一举。

C- I tried to like this one. I really did. Having seen Drive My Car (also by director Ryusuki Hamaguchi), I knew this was going to be slow, but as long as it was still investing like DMC I didn't think it would be a problem. But I never got invested, no matter how hard I tried. The first hour I found really tough to get through since more than half of that time frame is this session at a physical therapy class or whatever that was, and it wasn't like DMC where you could technically lose the first forty minutes but in doing so you would sacrifice some crucial and rich characterization, because during this session we learn nothing major about anyone. But since I had another four hours to go I wasn't judging it too harshly since I figured the pacing would pick up once the story kicked in. But sadly, even when the story did actually start, I was still unable to get into it. So for the past FIVE HOURS I've been bored out of my mind. I'm glad that this brought Hamaguchi into the international spotlight and that Drive My Car received major awards buzz which resulted in a Best Picture nomination, but that doesn't make me like THIS five hour slog any more then I do.

I pressed play and damn, 5 hours of film made me think like it was a vital decision whether I would embark on this journey or live in peace, and perhaps fortunately (or unfortunately) I chose to watch, and now I just want to go home, sleep and make my mind think that this will regulate my sleep, but at least it will give me the rest I need. I should clarify that I didn't watch the whole movie in one sitting, not even in a single day, of course, and something tells me that some fanatics will comment that this was the reason I didn't like it so much, but damn, I'm not going to do that, I'm sorry. I watched about 3 hours of the movie today to finish it and I can't say if it was good or bad, but actually something in me makes me want to be sure that it wasn't enjoyable, and I agree with that something. I wanted to stop watching the movie several times and I don't know why I didn't. I think for some reason I expected it to be as good as "Eureka," which has a similar vibe, but this one is something much more distinct. Affairs, slice of life, the drama of constantly dissatisfied adult life and friendships—all of this makes up "Happy Hour" and the narratives of the four characters. I think this is an attempt to immerse us as much as possible in everyone's lives and the melancholy that pervades the entire film, which is why it's so long. In fact, the character development and the acting (including amateur performances, but still very good) are very good elements, but at the same time, I felt like I was traveling and traveling and didn't reach a destination with the plot. It's not that "Happy Hour" is necessarily bad; I understand that it's so acclaimed not only because cinephiles love a tediously long film (I say this respectfully, okay?) and, on top of that, a Japanese one, but because it's clearly a strong, well-made work with a unique approach; truly impressive. But personally, I can't like it. The story didn't grab my attention, I lost interest at numerous points, and despite appreciating several aspects like the well-done production, I couldn't connect with the film and I think I wasted my time watching the whole thing. I'm sorry.

Tenu et gardé par ses cinq heures pléthoriques, Happy Hour se présente comme un geste de cinéma faussement modeste, cherchant à surplomber le groupe de femmes qu’il observe et l’urbanité japonaise qu’il retient en toile de fond. Pourtant, cette durée-fleuve ne dilate pas le sentiment, elle l’érode, l’éparpille dans des plans savamment composés, dans la brume des paysages et l’étirement des scènes. L’on croit d’abord que cette prolifération de paroles, d’instants suspendus, finira par fissurer les corps, par rompre l’équilibre que cristallise la fameuse séquence de l’atelier — véritable pilier dramaturgique. Mais c’est la réverbération du temps lui-même qui consume le film, non ses rares secousses émotionnelles. Hamaguchi ne prolonge plus le temps pour en éprouver la densité, mais pour en vérifier la lassitude — comme si le flot continu de paroles finissait par devenir son propre barrage, une écluse mélancolique où se perdent les larmes promises.

50/100 Gonna miss those nine blissful years when I resided among the 99.9999% of humanity that's just never seen this film, rather than being literally the only person I know who has seen it and thinks it's roughly three hours too long. (Cutting that much would still leave it longer than Tokyo Story, which runs 136 minutes.) Thought I might have written something down when I bailed—after nearly two hours!—back in 2016, but if so I can't find it; the gist would have been that I got quite intrigued during the lengthy "finding your center" seminar (despite hating that sort of thing IRL) but was subsequently bored into a stupor by the almost equally lengthy café outing that follows, which to my mind could not more obviously be extremely unfocused improv. (Actually, it'd probably be even more obvious if I understood Japanese. But that comes across even via subtitles.) Don't think I learned back then that Hamaguchi built the entire movie around some sort of acting workshop, using the non-pros who'd taken it, but man alive does that make sense. There's just so much here that seems inessential, suggesting a group of people who are roaming around trying to find the story they're ostensibly telling, and who can't bear to part with any discoveries made along the way. And yet at the same time, I still have very little sense, after more than five hours spent in her company, of who Fumi (the one who works at the seminar space) even is. It takes a damn strong actor to make recessive look dynamic, and Maiko Mihara isn't up to the task; at one point, Sakurako incredulously asks I think it's Kohei something like "Do you really not know why [Fumi]'s angry?" and quite frankly I didn't know either. Compounding that frustration, Jun, by far the most compelling character (thanks in large part to Rira Kawamura's effortless screen presence; she's the only one of the main quartet whom I'd have counseled to consider a career in acting), disappears from the movie about halfway through, her place effectively taken by her weirdly robotic husband*. Even after she's gone, the most dramatically potent scenes involve her absence, which would be fine and dandy and maybe even L'Avventura -esque were they not dwarfed by other, less interesting matters (e.g. Sakurako's teenage son getting his girlfriend pregnant, though Hamaguchi uses that to give Jun one last appearance). Jun's efforts to escape her loveless marriage, and how that affects her circle of friends, fires on all cylinders at all times; the film's single best moment is a close-up of Sakurako asleep that's overlaid with the sound of Jun's ferry rumbling, from the previous scene, with the noise abruptly cutting off when her eyes open. By contrast, the other two marriages, while clearly not entirely healthy, get so little comparative attention—remember, this is a five-hour movie! it's not as if there's no time—that it's downright odd when they suddenly become hugely significant in the last half hour or so, as if this had always primarily been a film about women in unhappy wedlock. (How Akari fits into that schema, I have no idea. Hugging her timid fellow nurse does not qualify.) On the contrary, it's just sort of about whatever it feels like being about (quite possibly the appeal for some), which shifts from one extended setpiece to the next. Too busy and melodramatic to work as Rivette-style durational mystique (though the initial seminar, with its chair-balancing and quasi-telepathic exercises, seemed to promise exactly that), too rambling to satisfy as either a narrative or a four-way character study. Somehow, against all logic, Happy Hour manages to be both bloated and skimpy. There's definitely a good normal-length film in there, but I kinda resent having been forced to wade through so much ehh to find it. The good news is that, after failing to connect with Hamaguchi for four straight acclaimed features (I'm also one of the only known mixed votes on Drive My Car ), I've finally found one that I loved almost from start to finish. The bad news is: Almost. Too soon to kick off a debate about Evil Does Not Exist 's ending. * That dude's a perfect example of what bugs me about Hamaguchi's approach here. It makes very little sense that Fumi would ask a biologist to conduct a literary Q&A, even in desperation, and it makes no sense at all that she would turn to this particular walking monotone, with whose creepy lack of personality I'm fairly confident she's familiar given that he's married to one of her best friends. Obviously Fumi would do it herself, but Hamaguchi's doing whatever he can think of to unite disparate narrative threads, so she begs off on the grounds that she wasn't paying close enough attention, okay sure Jan. And then the guy's somehow perceived by everyone (including critics I've read and the Wikipedia plot summary) as having done a surprisingly good job, when in fact he arguably talks more than the author does. (For the Q&A's first half, that ratio is like 10:1; she can't get a word in and doesn't even try. Not what I'm looking for as an audience member, but then I hate Q&As.)

Le film a bien des qualités avec cette manière qu'il a de tracer sa propre route dans la cartographie de relations toutes délétères et vouées à l'échec, cela résulte en une espèce de mélancolie terrible qui traverse le film. L'impression de personnages tous isolés dans des espaces singuliers et incapables d'en sortir (ou trop brièvement). En cela le rapport avec le workshop de la première partie est passionnant, un travail de rapport à l'autre qui prouvera sans cesse son impossibilité. Cependant, d'une part le film a quelque chose d'énervant dans son aspect purement japonais, un peuple quand même dominé par des handicapés sociaux, qui donnent souvent envie de tous les envoyer chier. Tu crèves un peu d'envie que les personnages explosent, gesticulent, hurlent, se battent au lieu de rester droit comme des piquets en répétant sumimasen en se prosternant de la tête. C'est vraiment culturel mais bon, le film expose des relations de couple cauchemardesques, intégralement basées sur la frustration et le non-dit. Difficile d'universaliser ça au reste du monde. Du coup ça me laisse sans cesse à distance de personnages qui semblent bloqués dans des schémas horriblement figés. Après ça reste 4 beaux personnages même si paradoxalement je trouve presque plus intéressant les personnages masculins, jamais véritablement jugés ou du moins qui semblent simplement ne pas réaliser leurs erreurs mais restent des êtres sensibles un peu perdus (très belle scène du salary man qui éclate en sanglots au milieu de la rue). D'autre part, le film est quand même très chiant. Je trouve que le film justifie jamais sa durée excessive (et je suis quelqu'un qui adore certains films très longs comme Satantango par ex). Déjà j'ai fait un calcul rapide mais pour donner une idée il y a trois scènes qui durent en tout 1h30, le workshop c'est 30min, la scène de discussion interminable au bar juste après c'est 25min et l'ignoble scène de la lecture du roman (enfin ignoble en terme de durée, c'est une jolie scène à la base) dure près de 40min... Donc à partir de là je veux bien qu'on creuse la matière, qu'on tente d'aller au bout de scènes filmées en temps réel mais quand les dialogues sont plats comme la poitrine de Keira Knightley et que la mise en scène est aux abonnés absentes je décroche très très rapidement. Je veux dire des scènes de dialogues dans des bars interminables filmées en plans fixes, Hong Sang Soo construit ses films autour de ça et jamais je me fais chier comme je me suis fait chier ici. Et tout est un peu comme ça, impression que chaque scène devient trop longue à un moment et finit par être chiante, surtout que l'ensemble est tellement dévitalisé, tellement apathique et neurasthénique que bon 5h20 ça devient vite intolérable. Bref bien déçu vu la réputation du film et surtout vu que j'ai adoré Asako vu à Cannes qui me semble infiniment supérieur (sur un sujet d'ailleurs extrêmement similaire). Film d'une légèreté romantique délicieuse mais traversé aussi d'un mélancolie existentielle terrible.

Mis bout à bout, le projet impressionne : une narration audacieuse, un regard déjà singulier sur le monde, porté par une foi dans la puissance de la poésie, de l'écoute, des trajectoires personnelles. Comment se connaître et s'aimer soi-même, comment composer avec l'autre ? Hamaguchi est un cinéaste profondément philosophique, et qui l'assume — sa grâce est de rendre cette philosophie accessible. Il aime aussi inviter d'autres œuvres dans son cinéma, avec exigence : le théâtre dans "Drive My Car" ou "Soudain", et ici la lecture intégrale d'un texte intime signé d'une jeune romancière, suivie d'un débat avec elle. Postures clivantes, qu'on pourra juger anti cinématographiques, mais qui définissent son geste. Les moments les plus forts sont sans doute les affrontements. Je pense à cette soirée, après un atelier étrange où les quatre amies apprennent à écouter le corps des autres, où le divorce tenu secret de l'une d'elles finit par affleurer et fait éclater les tensions pour des raisons parfaitement inattendues, qui tiennent à la susceptibilité, à la jalousie. À partir de là, ce groupe qu'on imaginait uni vole en éclats, puis tente de se reformer sans jamais vraiment y parvenir. Beaucoup diront que le format tient davantage de la série ; je dirais simplement que "Senses" est un film trop long, parce que l'émotion s'y dilue sur une durée qu'il ne parvient pas à tenir. Les ramifications montent si haut qu'on finit par perdre de vue le tronc : l'amitié et ses perceptions divergentes au sein d'un groupe de femmes, la solidarité, l'amour, bref la vie, ou comment la reconstruire dans le Japon d'aujourd'hui, entre famille, amitié et travail. Dans ses œuvres suivantes, même plus courtes comme "Contes du hasard et autres fantaisies", l'artisan Hamaguchi devient orfèvre : l'émotion se densifie de film en film sans rien sacrifier des audaces de mise en scène. "Senses" n'atteint pas encore cette puissance. J'y vois pourtant la matrice de "Soudain", si différent dans son sujet mais si proche dans sa foi en la conversation comme événement : en resserrant sur deux personnages ce que "Senses" dispersait sur quatre trajectoires, Hamaguchi parvient enfin à tenir l'émotion sur la durée. Reste qu’il compose dans "Senses" avec une galerie de femmes complexes, autrement plus fines que les clichés dont se contentent la plupart des fictions, et touche à une vérité profonde dans la représentation de l'humain. On sent l'artiste au travail. Parler de brouillon serait injuste tant il contient de belles choses ; disons plutôt que les films qu'il signera ensuite, avec des ingrédients similaires, seront encore plus émotionnels, profonds, évocateurs.

Director Ryusuke Hamaguchi chronicles the friendship between four women in their late thirties, navigating their family lives, personal relationships and sexual dramas, as well as their emotional and moral conflicts. "Happy Hours" utilizes art film devices on the typical soap opera structure, which rather than being unravelled over an endless run of episodes progresses over an extended, and frankly excessive, length of over five hours. Hamaguchi deviates from the norm by lending legitimacy to the intricate plot through extended dialogue sequences and intellectually stimulating elements, highlighting the breakdown of communication and the disintegration of monogamy in the modern era. However, "Happy Hour"'s blend of faux naturalism and soap operatic excess often teeters on pretentiousness, constantly risking to devolve into self-parody. Recommended related viewing: "Rocco and His Brothers" (dir. Luchino Visconti, 1960)

It's definitely not a bad movie but I feel like so many of these reviews are more of a badge of honor for completing the five hour marathon of a film than any thoughts of actual analysis or substance. I definitely think it's worth checking out if you have interest but just go in with neutral expectations. I found the main four interesting and realistic. It feels rare to see women above 25 portrayed with such care. Towards the end, I did feel like each woman was my real friend. Some of the minor characters like Yukino and Daiko are pleasant surprises as well. The conflicts are mature and engaging without being "soapy". The conversations are well-written and realistic in their length. Rather than being truncated, we hear everybword and see every expression adding to the immersion in the world. So why then, does the ecstatic letterboxd praise feel so forced? Skim through the reviews and the praise feels vague words used include: "subtle", "dense" and "rewarding". It's possible for something to be subtle and dense but still practice brevity. It ends up feeling like the writing was trying to address too much on such complex topics but just became bloated and disjointed, extending the runtime to over-explain rather than leave anything to the viewer. The most egregious is the masturbatory "book reading" scene in which an author reads a short story (for a droning 10 minutes), recieves praise for 5 minutes and then explains her thoughts in an interview about the meaning of the story with themes that mirror those in the film. Finally, describing the experience as "rewarding" is the same as calling running a marathon or going on an expensive medidation retreat "rewarding". It turns the film into this bizarre "flex" where everyone is patting each other's back for making out to the other side and pretending it's some great revelation when it's largely average. Which is sad because I think the runtime is exactly what kept it from its masterpiece potential. I wish it was executed as one short or full length movie per woman rather than the slog it turned out to be. I think I will revisit this when I'm older, wiser and maybe more patient, but at my current age of 28, I'm kind of over these self-important film-bro type movies. I will check out this director's other films as this one has peaked my interest. I would love nothing more than to be proven wrong about my current opinions!

“Nice to meet you on the 25th year". I caught glimpses of greatness in the script of Happy Hour especially when it evoked memories from other Japanese literary classics.  Let's say Jun's failed marriage is quite similar to that of Rinko in Junichi Watanabe's Lost Paradise, for they are both married to an unfeeling scientist, who is relentlessly chasing after them despite the pending divorce. As Happy Hour took a distressing and existential turn, the change in narrative style also reminded me of the works of Murakami Haruki (which unfortunately does not vibe with me). Every real-time sequence initially felt so elegant and profound as the characters exchanged thoughts. But under the disguise of a lighthearted J-drama, Hamaguchi is plotting something more ambitious with the challenging 5-hour screen time. Jun's divorce and mysterious vanishing propelled every unexpected twist and turn in the second half. These shockers although unpredictable, do not seem to be out of place thanks to the deliberate script. Say Ukai's spontaneity has already been foreshadowed by his sister in an earlier scene after the workshop. And the writings are on the wall for these married couples who are going to find their relationship in crisis. But somehow, as the passage of time flows the energy from the script also dissipates and I am not sure where Hamaguchi is getting to. I just don't feel Happy Hour can be boiled down to a core idea, probably that is how life gonna unfold, but it can also be frustrating to watch.

Hamaguchi's patient ability to connect to the interior lives of his characters is second to none. He uses time like an archaeologist's brush to clear the dust and reveal the truth. I appreciate the time when spending it with the character's lives and their interactions. The characters are sometimes unlikable, but that is part of the film's charm. I also love the scenery whether it's the countryside of Japan or just walking out of a train station and crossing a bridge. Indoors, it gets much less interesting, often resembling the flat documentary style and setting of episodes of The Office. Forgivable, but not compelling, particularly for long, long scenes. The unfortunate part is that the plots of this and other Hamaguchi movies revolve heavily around a handful of soap opera level incidents or contrivances and moments that drag me out of this wonderful, complex world he portrays. I see his most recent movie is leaner, so maybe he is evolving. I'll give that one a shot.

While I love long films, there are times I'm daunted by the runtime depending on the film itself. 'Happy Hour' is a 5+ hour drama around the small lives of four women. That's right: just when you finished a 2 1/2 hour movie, you got another 2 1/2 hour movie to watch plus an additional seventeen minutes of your choice. Despite the praise, I'm rather mixed, but I can understand both opinionated sides, even if I lean a bit more on one. It's rather a visual novel: exploring their lives in full detail, every scene taking its time with its slower pacing, making sure the audience is living with them, details hidden till revealed, and really loves the leads by delaying the conflict till around the eighty-minute mark. My favorite would be Akari; she's a nurse and I found her more interesting in personality, although Sakurako's storyline kicks in gear around the three-hour mark, and Jun is the one with her conflict; Fumi's show comes in later. While I appreciate its commitment in itself, did it really need to be 317 minutes long? I don't think so. Cutting two hours or so would make it an abridged version, sure, but there were several times I felt unengaged and even bored because it felt rather dry and tedious, in my opinion. The length basically doesn't earn itself from its script, and I felt something rich and beautiful was missing. At least it wasn't sappy - far from it. 'Yi Yi' is almost three hours, but I never thought it was a bog as it manages to tell its epic slice-of-life story without sacrificing too much; 'Happy Hour', on the other hand, is too precious of its memories all the time. Some don't think it's a big deal, but I thought the cinematography was kinda boring. Let me say this: the framing and composition are well-done, but the lack of color grading and using only the white balance, I assume, got tiring and plain after a while. Also, the sound editing isn't amazing, but I imagine the budget was much smaller, and I've heard editing is expensive. I can see both sides defending for what they stand: either a reflective, human masterpiece or a bloated, self-indulgent movie. As for me, it's a risky experiment that doesn't fully pay off for me, where I see a great three-hour film hidden within what I thought was the editor's cut. A minor recommendation.

During the latter half of the expedition that is Happy Hour , there is a scene where a young author named Ms. Nose is criticized for having read her book to an audience in a monotone voice. She answers that since she knew the characters she wrote so well, and all of the emotions are on the page, no matter what vocal inflections she adds, the importance is found in the words. Happy Hour hinges on words and communication. For what's basically a five-hour-long monologue how could it not be about these things? The story follows four women who vocalize their anxieties to everyone except the people who these actual anxieties originate, mostly their husbands. The story becomes how communication gets lost in a marriage. Saying a couple of words as a husband and wife pass by each other around the breakfast table is not the kind of interaction that can sustain a marriage. Before long the important needs of these women go unaddressed and they realize they could do better. I like where Hamaguchi takes the story. In a very Bergman-esque fashion, he captures the female perspective with confidence. However, to draw on how Ms. Nose reads her book in a monotone way, the rest of the movie features the most unemotive acting I've ever seen. I believe this was done purposefully to show the true emptiness behind each woman's marriage. None of the cast are trained actors either for this reason. The scene I brought up basically literalizes the intent of emphasizing the dialogue. For my personal enjoyment of this film, I couldn't get compelled to care about any of these characters for the lack of them feeling like people I know or acting like actual people at all. A character would be told about how their partner wants a divorce and they would wear an awkward blank stare. Outside of the film's length showcasing an incremental decline of each character's relationship with their spouse, I did not see the need for a five-hour project. I would've settled for three. I think for anything dialogue-heavy, talented actors really go a long way to sell key emotional moments. A lot of the time I couldn't read what emotion a character was showing, rendering the point of the scene mute. Hamaguchi builds a believable world around its characters, but there was so much more to explore, things that were left unsaid, which makes me think that the five hour runtime could've been used more effectively.

I enjoyed this dialogue-driven flick in bursts and flashes -- more than I can say Hamaguchi's other big hit, Drive My Car -- whenever it really productively explored the ways we do or don't communicate with one another. I just wish it wasn't five-plus bloody hours. I know, I know: the entire movie is fundamentally about the ways we do or don't communicate, so my statement above can seem silly. The kick is that it does so with varying degrees of clarity or focus throughout its painful runtime, and I found myself rapt in those stretches where it really was tackling the concepts head-on. So yes, then this thing gets into the meaning of what it is to be in a relationship, and how we center ourselves while also supporting other people? Brilliant. I wasn't sold on its tactics at first, but the way Hamaguchi puts you through these trust exercises, seemingly without purpose, and then has a participant criticize the instructor with the same thoughts as I had, only to have the purpose hinted at a bit more firmly -- well, let's just say it helped crystallize the point of the film. It's not that I'm an idiot; I understand and appreciate some artistic metaphor and allusion. It's when people are staring in silence for five minutes, or moving into much less direct tangents that I find myself being pulled into areas of the film that work for me much less well, and that I think is where the majority of this thing spends its time. Ryusuke Hamaguchi is a student of Yasujiro Ozu, Mikio Naruse and classic Hollywood and this is obvious even from his first important feature film. "Happy Hour" is a 5-hour film based entirely on dialogue and interaction between characters. It's a depiction of the daily life of four women in modern-day Japan, not as multi-layered as it promises to be, but still very intriguing, thanks to Hamaguchi's mise-en-scene and the exceptional dialogue. The film takes its time and feels like a big novel or a long haiku poem, where you get to know the characters in every aspect of their existence and not just in the events a normal movie would consist of. The sweet music score, the solid performances and the fine editing are among the film's advantages, but I can't say I didn't feel exhausted at certain points. Far from being a masterpiece, "Happy Hour" is indeed an example of Hamaguchi's style and a preparation for possibly better films in the near future.

Happy ist in „Happy Hour“ nur eins: 4 Freundinnen Ende der 30iger sind Freundinnen. „Ich wünschte, ich würde in den dreißigern auch noch 3 neue so gute Freundinnen finden.“ Das sagt eine unbekannte Frau im Bus zu einer der Hauptpersonen am Ende von Kapitel 2. Mein „Happy“ Moment. Ansonsten gibt es in diesem 5 Stunden und 17 Minuten (!) Epos jede Menge unhappy, unhappy, unhappy Hours. Hamaguchi zeichnet das Bild einer kaputten Gesellschaft die längst verlernt hat miteinander zu kommunizieren. „Ein Königreich für den Urlaub oder die eine Stunde abschalten am Tag“ - da ist sie wieder die „Happy Hour“. In diesen kleinen Momenten können unsere vier Hauptprotagonistinnen das Leben annähernd genießen, bevor es wieder in die 23 Stunden unhappy Hour des Tages geht. Insofern wohl doch ein Titel über den sich jemand Gedanken gemacht hat. Und wie fand dich das ganze jetzt so? Happy Happy Unhappy würde ich sagen. Die exorbitante Laufzeit (ob das wirklich fast fünfeinhalb Stunden sein müssen für den Inhalt darüber würde ich schon mal diskutieren aber geschenkt) geht relativ schnell vorüber, der Stil des wirklich sehr nahbar umgesetzten Realismus ist gelungen und einige Einstellungen (z.B. der Beginn des Films im Tunnel oder die „Wasserfallstadt“ haben mir sehr gefallen). Da schwenke ich aber auch zu meinen Kritikpunkten. Von diesen ruhigen Minuten mit tollen Bildern hätte ich gerne mehr gehabt (ist ja nicht so, dass man in dem Film keine Zeit hat). Stattdessen gibt es dann einen 20 minütigen Literaturvortrag vor weißer Wand, wie man denn diese Stadt so wahrgenommen hat. Hamaguchi sei ein großer Bewunderer von Eric Rohmer – in diesem Zusammenhang gibt das dann natürlich Sinn. Aber ob ich auf so einen Eric Rohmer Wasserfalldialoge im Realismus des 21. Jahrhundert aus Japan über 5 Stunden gewartet habe – bin mir nicht so sicher. Gerade auch die „Workshopszene“ am Anfang des Films strapaziert da schon manche Nerven (soll sie ja auch). Auch übergeordnete Themen waren für über 5 Stunden für mich etwas dünn. Da wäre die Scheidung die über allem schwebt und eben die gescheiterte Kommunikationsgesellschaft. Im Grunde auch teilweise ein Porträt, wie einen die Gesellschaft auffrisst und man eben ein paar Verbündete braucht, die einem die eigenen Fehler verzeihen. Und Lügen und Fehler gibt es hier viele. Lösungen gibt es dagegen keine. Der Mensch läuft schon lange seine unhappy Hours auf Autopilot, hat sich arrangiert, kann nicht mehr verzeihen und versucht aus seiner einen Happy Hour so viel Lebenssaft zu saugen, dass es wieder für die nächsten 23 reicht. Ich kann für mich auch sagen, dass ich für keine der 4 Hauptprotagonistinnen besonders große Sympathien aufbringen konnte (für die Nebencharaktere allerdings auch nicht wirklich). Ein sperriges, authentisches, negatives und interessantes Werk. Angesichts der Tatsache, dass ich den Ostasiatischen Film aber besonders im arthousigen Bereich für mich mit am Stärksten halte muss ich für mich sagen, dass dieser Film dann eher auf der schwächeren Seite steht. Bong Joon-ho, Zhangke aber vor allem der als Vergleich für mich recht passende Koe-ede haben da mit weniger Zeitaufwand die für mich einfach viel eindringlicheren und stärkeren Werke gedreht. Sollte ich jedoch jemals in meinem Leben vor einer Scheidung stehen und dabei auch noch um die 40 Jahre rum sein – ich würde anders über diesen Film schreiben.

So, how do I represent the world, and not just myself? Happy Hour , more like Somber Five Hours . Hamaguchi, you madman. An over five hour movie that's more or less made up of conversation after conversation sounds like a death sentence for engagement. Instead, while I wasn't truly wowed by it like seemingly all of my mutuals on here were, I was at least impressed by it more often than not. It's through these moments that the characters share, and what they talk about, that they are able to work through the woes of their lives. It is through talking that they will seemingly be taking a new path towards being better. Do I think Hamaguchi has portrayed that better in his other films at a much shorter length? Absolutely. I do also think that being able to make the ending to a film that's this long feel in some way cathartic, and it's not because you are in relief that it's finally over, that's still an achievement. I think also especially with intense family drama going on with myself currently, the moments reflecting on love and divorce had extra poignancy. The story of four friends in Kobe and their disintegrating relationships amidst endless and varied attempts to communicate. Akari is divorced and outspoken, a strong nurse with an empathy deficit. Sakurako is a put-upon housewife with an ungenerous husband and a teenager (who in turn has a unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend). Fumi is a childless curator with a husband who's more a roommate than a romantic (or, at least, his romantic affections are directed elsewhere). And Jun is divorcing her spouse, a cold blooded scientist who hasn't harmed her but won't ever let her go, even if she has to fly into hiding with her unborn child. I've seen "Happy Hour" described as novelistic and that's true, but also a coded way of excusing its 317-minute run time. Just as much of a novel, however, the film reminds me of a workshop, and indeed two very long stretches of the movie are centered around performances of sorts at Fumi's arts space, PORTO (not to mention the extended, fractious discussions after both). Perhaps fitting as I understand that Ryusuke Hamaguchi developed the script through improvisational exercises with his non-professional actresses. Not entirely successful in its own right, as the dyads can feel a bit obvious and the pacing languorous, but I'm convinced that this work is a rehearsal for a compelling cinematic voice.

When a movie is over, let's say, two and a half hours long, the length becomes a key question to consider. Does this movie need to be this long? What is gained in that length? Would it be better, tighter, more incisive at a shorter length, or should it be even longer to really achieve something more resonant? With Happy Hour, the single longest film I've ever watched at north of five hours long, it's a question you have to consider. Ryusuke Hamaguchi isn't shy with his runtimes, with Drive My Car (to my mind his masterpiece and the best film of the 2020s) stretching a somewhat slight Murakami short story to over three hours, for instance. In all cases, I think the length is ultimately to his movies' and interests' benefit. He is radically in love with humanity and his way in is through sensitivity, nuance and observational verisimilitude. These characters, who deepen to a truly profound degree despite their situations being quotidian, come to life in a way that may not have been possible in a conventional runtime, at least not to this degree. There are two epic-lengthed scenes in the film, one in the first half (a somewhat woo-woo "centering" workshop) and a short story reading/Q&A in the second half that in any other movie would be a context for a more "important" scene while allowing for some crucial symbolism, and while both things are also true here, by allowing them to play out in so much detail, Hamaguchi achieves a (somewhat less successful and more proterozoic) form of later experiments with this in, say, the Uncle Vanya subplot of Drive My Car or the council meetings of Evil Does Not Exist: they aren't just trite metaphorical gestures, they are part of a giant tapestry of human experience, and that is just a really cool, singular approach to filmmaking that I find myself once again besotted with. I do think his later films find a way to do all of this with a little bit more narrative economy and propulsion, and while the style here is sturdy and classical (excellent compositions, but without that little extra that make his recent films some of the most incredibly gorgeous films in contemporary cinema), aesthetically he would make huge strides with his 2020s output, especially with regards to his collaboration with Eiko Ishibashi. As a burgeoning Hamaguchi Head, though, I was very glad to have seen this and to truly luxuriate in Hamaguchi's unvarnished but incredibly generous world.

One of Happy Hour's first extended scenes draws the audience into a metadiscourse on the failures of ordinary communication, laying out the film's ambition: to unravel them with enough restraint to preserve realism and enough conviction to allow that realism to admit genuine transformation. Characters often tell white lies because they're afraid others won't accept their truth, but the truth revealed in those falsehoods exceeds what remains unspoken. Whatever remains unspoken forms the tension explored by the subsequent scene, with every interaction reintroducing characters who become infinitely more complex as the film progresses. If you think you know them at any point, something new is revealed that makes you realize this is impossible. But nothing you know about them changes; none of it loses its truth or significance. You just realize how small your perception is and how much larger it's capable of being. Their interactions are intimate enough that we're still given plenty of painful clarity. We see people clinging to assumptions, hoping others will arrive at the same conclusions on their own; unhappiness neglected by false hope, love and hurt too obvious for those closest to them to notice. So when the characters finally speak aloud the words we've known to be true for quite some time, it's a revelation. All the little things appear monumental when they're no longer concealed by the internalization of their supposed insignificance. Real change is suddenly possible, but first we have to sit with things as they actually are, now that we're finally able to do so.

I ordered a region-free DVD player just so I could watch this intimate, five-hour-plus epic of domestic life from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, who’s quickly become one of my favorite working directors (and quite possibly my very favorite). Two discs, three viewing sessions, and one day of rumination later, I can say that Happy Hour is an essential part of Hamaguchi’s filmography, thoroughly imbued with the intelligence and humanity that mark his extraordinary recent work ( Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy , Drive My Car , Evil Does Not Exist ). I have a few hesitations about some recurring elements that, despite the massive runtime, feel less consequential than I’d like them to be (guy who runs the New Age workshop that we experience in full, I’m looking at you). But on the whole, I was happy to be immersed in a film that values the mundane but that, in its very form, departs so strikingly from ordinary moviegoing experience. A few areas of thought: * Loved how completely female friendship permeates the film, even through some long stretches in which Akari, Jun, Sakurako, and Fumi remain apart. I thought from time to time about Virginia Woolf’s The Waves , in which the friendship between six characters who meet as children and interact only intermittently as adults forms a vessel that gives life meaning, a structure of belonging that has no official sanction or force but remains a continuous source of identity. The slow pace of the film’s first two hours comes in part from how the women, preoccupied by and/or attempting to cover up unhappiness related to marriage, family life, and work, don’t communicate very openly with one another, but one senses how their bond might offer a framework for disruption or renewal. I found the middle hour, leading up to and immediately following the trip to the hot springs resort, most compelling for precisely this reason, as the women begin to prod each other—lovingly, but not always pleasantly—to speak beyond their learned inhibitions, to risk a more radical, unsettling kind of honesty with one another. * As for what the film has to say about gender, sex and sexuality, and Japan’s still conservative mores and laws around marriage and divorce: forceful stuff, appropriately stamped with the texture and complication of actual life. None of the heterosexual relationships in Happy Hour are satisfying in any way, and Jun’s refusal to submit herself to a marriage she’s come to experience as deadly—as she attests in court, he’s killed her by lack of conversation—acts as a catalyst for some of the other women to ask themselves questions about desire, need, and sacrifice that would otherwise remain encased in the “cotton wool” of the ordinary (I’m borrowing from Woolf again). Nevertheless, it’s not apparent that there are right or wrong choices for each of the women, merely that there are choices: whether one seeks a separation or a strategy for marital repair, one can do and say things beyond the routine and reassert a right to happiness, even when the path to happiness remains elusive. * On the related topic of expressivity: I understand that the stolid reserve of the women has a cultural element and that it makes key moments of breakdown or decisiveness all the more poignant. At times, though, the performances verge on illegibility, and in some of the more charged stretches of the last two hours, I couldn’t quite work out what the film was suggesting about self-possession under duress. It occurred to me that the restrained affect might be related to the film’s understanding of itself as a kind of literary text, too. The visiting writer who reads her short story aloud at the cultural institute where Fumi works is herself asked why she performs with so little emotion, and the answer is a fascinating one: she doesn’t want to pretend that she can inhabit all of her characters, and she thinks that a sort of presentational truth, one that simply delivers the words themselves, still carries all the requisite feeling. A version of this idea may apply to the film, too. In the relative absence of histrionics, perhaps we are better able to understand and internalize the accrued weight of what these women have carried in their lives, the unspectacular ways they have been subsumed into (but thankfully not consumed by) the everyday. * Lastly, about duration: yes, I do think this could be an hour or two shorter and it would work nearly as well. And yet, I think it’s important to say that this isn’t a miniseries in disguise. It’s a novelistic film, just as Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy is a filmic collection of short stories. Although I watched in installments, I felt the continuous logic of the film’s development, the way the friendship group’s warm, complex, fraught tangle shifted and reconstituted, and how it informed the dramas in the women’s individual lives. Though I found some parts of the film too languorous, a bit too repetitive or restrained, I also didn’t want to leave these characters in the end, with their understanding of themselves and the impact of some of their bolder, pattern-breaking choices still very much in progress. But that’s the truth in which I suspect Hamaguchi is most invested: whatever span of time one chooses for a story, markers like beginnings and endings are arbitrary impositions, creations dictated by narrative. Stratificato e ricco di dialoghi eccellenti, mantiene la classica firma dell’autore per tutto il tempo, rallentando e arenandosi un po’ in tutta la sezione legata al club di lettura e al discorso sull’artista e sul suo modo di vedere e trascrivere il mondo, che ho trovato abbastanza fine a se stessa e superflua. Per il resto, come già menzionato, è l’ennesimo film di un autore grandioso che da sempre prova di avere qualcosa da raccontare, intrattenendo (quasi) sempre anche nelle situazioni più improbabili. O filme é um emaranhado de situações e conversas sobre os mais diversos assuntos que vão girar em torno pricipalmente sobre relacionamentos. Seja o modo como nos relacionamos com nossos amores ou com nossos amigos e como o mundo acaba influenciando tudo isso. Cada uma das quatro amigas tem suas perspectivas sobre a vida e sobre si mesmas alteradas de forma significativa, o filme irá explorar como isso vai afetando seus relacionamentos. Grande parte dos assuntos levantados irão dizer a respeito do amor dentro de um relacionamento: por quanto tempo ele dura? inevitavelmente iremos estar nessas situações que as personagens se encontram? existe alguma maneira de salvar isso? Ao mesmo tempo que o filme expõe a importância de um relacionamento pelo lado positivo e pelo lado negativo, também acaba expondo outras questões que irão surgir quando não se está em um relacionamento, o que torna a abordagem do filme sobre esse assunto bem rica. Além disso, ainda existe uma atenção que é dada em como nosso trabalho e os demais relacionamentos que temos acaba afetando nossas vidas privadas, positivamente e negativamente. Mesmo que as cenas pareçam ser filmadas de um modo mais livre, dá pra notar que existe um cuidado na forma como são filmadas. Mesmo o filme abordando temas bem pesados e que possuam um tom triste, ele procura equilibrar com uma estética mais contemplativa. A forma como ele filma a natureza, como ele usa os locais para transmitir uma beleza intocável do mundo.

5 hours and 17 minutes of Ryusuke Hamaguchi´s gentle, authentic, and profound humanism. Following the trials and tribulations of four female friends in their 30s, “Happy Hour” is filled with nuanced characters, insightful observations, thought-provoking contemplations, and quiet beauty. It´s Hamaguchi´s first great movie, already showcasing the rewarding combination of truthful dialogue, understated yet captivating visual composition, and unhurried pacing that would later win him an Oscar for “Drive My Car”. Sure, some scenes go on for longer than they probably need to but overall, it´s refreshing that every scene gets room to breathe. The main character arcs are carefully developed and at the same time they´re so subtle that they don´t even feel like “arcs” but simply like real life. That´s one of Hamaguchi´s biggest strengths. He is one of those special filmmakers who make mundane everyday life feel noteworthy, interesting, and, well, cinematic. “Happy Hour” is a spellbinding experience. I didn´t even notice how invested I got in the lives of those four women; it just naturally happened. The film´s bittersweet and resonating meditation on friendship, romance, human connection, and the passage of time will linger in my mind for a while. Furthermore, the movie serves as a PSA about the pitfalls of Japanese divorce law and as a very nice portrait of Kobe (the city, not the basketball player).

It has been a joy and quite a chance experiment to follow Hamaguchi’s career backwards from Evil Does not Exist, Drive my Car, to Wheels of Fortune and Fantasy, and Happy Hour. Recently got a sneak peak of All of a Sudden as well. I’m dying to watch his even earlier films like Passion and Asako, and I don’t know how he can surprise me more. As you get more into his filmography you tap on your forehead and have this realization that this is a director who knows what he’s best at and keeps mastering his craft. His talent of scene construction, script writing, character building, momentum continuity just shines through the screen from the beginning like no other. Massive thanks to French New Wave, to Kurosawa, and Locarno film festival for providing the inspiration and stage for Hamaguchi to leave marks in film history. I wonder if the title Happy Hour is the exact translation from the Japanese title or if there’s nuance. I hate that in American (?) culture it has a rather superficial meaning. The length of the film… I think I felt it was halfway after two hours ish, the typical length for an entire feature film, which was so surprising, you can’t resist your urge to check on time when the movie’s bad, and this one I even needed to calculate a bathroom break (when are they not talking!!? Haha). Hamaguchi has the ability of writing dialogue that run smoothly, you would speak like that in daily life, they can be philosophical but have the sprinkle of mundane. And when they are going they struck you, when they stop they linger. They are not fast words with volume like maybe Linklater films, and the characters speak in a flat tone, with breaks, it’s really interesting I wonder how much of it is directors decision. Cinematographer has easy time with Hamaguchi project maybe haha, shots are so simple not dreamy flowy etc, they can even be problematic by the industry standards? Especially in the workshop scene (much of time the window light overpower and you can’t see faces at all, it’s dark). But it serves Hamaguchi’s style so well. I like the framing, I like when the director stare into the camera moments are happening, I wonder how much style Hamaguchi developed already and carried forward from his documentary projects. After a Hamaguchi film, you are not so sure if humanity is good or bad, whether we should keep on having hopes or diving into despair. But you know for sure that humanity is there and it’s worth keeping looking into it and looking after it.

Je dirais pas que c’est excellentissime du début à la fin, j’ai en effet ressenti quelques longueurs (surtout dans la deuxième partie) mais qu’est-ce que j’ai pris du plaisir à habiter ce film et à rentrer dans les conflits intérieurs de ses personnages, je les ai trouvés tellement concrets et vivants dans tous leurs aspects, qu’ils soient beaux ou biscornues que j’y m’y suis beaucoup attaché. En 5h de film Hamaguchi se permet de faire durer de nombreuses scènes et situations très longtemps, celles-ci se dépliants lentement mais sûrement au cours du visionnage, sans jamais forcer le pas. Il en ressort un sentiment de réel et de sincérité très fort, on est enveloppé et fasciné par ce qu’on voit. Le film a une respiration lente, renforçant encore plus les moments de trouble intense qui le parsèment, toujours présentés sobrement sur un ton calfeutré. Au de-là de son dispositif, le film est avant tout une histoire de femmes dans la société japonaise d’aujourd’hui. Au travers des quatre héroïnes on explore la condition féminine dans la vie maritale et amoureuse, dans la vie famille mais aussi dans l'amitié. La frustration, les non-dits, les jalousies et les désillusions tapissent les existences de ces quatre femmes tout à fait ordinaires et chacune y répond différemment. L’aspect le plus marquant étant peut-être le divorce d’une d’entre elle, déclencheur de nombreux questionnements au sein du groupe d’amies mais aussi, au Japon, un système absurde qui peut obliger une femme à rester aux côtés d’un mari qu’elle souhaite pourtant quitter du moment qu’elle est jugée fautive devant le tribunal. En bref un film marquant, long et doux-amer. Du grand Hamaguchi je te kiffe mon gars je te passe la bise.

A Kobe quattro amiche prossime ai quarant'anni condividono da anni un legame profondo, fatto di confidenze, abitudini e silenzi, vedendosi regolarmente per trascorrere del tempo soltanto tra loro. Quando Jun annuncia improvvisamente alle sodali l'intenzione di divorziare, Akari, Sakurako e Fumi si ritrovano costrette a fare i conti con le fragilità delle proprie esistenze, tra i rispettivi matrimoni in crisi e la solitudine di chi ancora l'amore lo cerca, ritrovandosi davanti a un bivio che fino ad allora avevano preferito ignorare. Più che raccontare una storia, Ryūsuke Hamaguchi osserva il modo in cui le relazioni possano cambiare impercettibilmente da un momento all'altro, trasformando un legame d'amicizia in un viaggio emotivo di rara intensità. Cinque ore e diciassette minuti di durata per un film dove dialoghi, silenzi e gesti quotidiani acquistano un significato sempre nuovo, riflettendo sulla comunicazione e sulla percezione del tempo. Alcune scene sono lunghissime e non nascondono nulla, restituendo un'intimità quasi documentaristica che permette di esplorare le emozioni e le dinamiche di chi (ci) vive accanto, in un Giappone dove spesso è la distanza sociale e affettiva a caratterizzare i rapporti, familiari e non. Con quattro straordinarie protagoniste, tutte attrici non professioniste, scelte al termine del laboratorio di recitazione da cui il progetto stesso ha preso forma.

Clocking in at over five hours, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (Happī Ā) is a quiet, monumental masterpiece of slow-cinema intimacy that feels less like watching a scripted movie and more like observing real lives unfold in unhurried, real time. Set in Kobe, the film follows a tight-knit circle of four women in their late 30s whose long-standing dynamics fracture when one of them suddenly reveals she is undergoing a messy divorce prompting the remaining three to re-examine their own stifled desires, marriages, and personal truths. What makes the film so uniquely captivating is Hamaguchi’s extraordinary process: developed through acting workshops with non-professional actors, the performances possess an astonishing, naturalistic grace (jointly earning all four lead actresses the Best Actress award at Locarno). Extended sequences like a fascinating body-listening workshop or a literary reading are allowed to breathe so fully that minor shifts in conversation carry the emotional impact of major plot twists. It’s an epic, exquisitely patient exploration of female friendship, emotional honesty, and the quiet compromises of adulthood.

The film’s raw portrayal of reality—and its subtle reflection of Japanese cultural tendencies toward non-verbal communication—kept pressing on me with quiet intensity throughout the entire film.

What I did and what I reccomend is getting a laptop set up with the movie and an HDMI cable and plugging both a good TV and your laptop to a side of the HDMI and then the movie will show up on your TV. After all, this movie is notoriously hard to find and the Internet Archive is free/ HAPPY HOUR REVIEW: I want to preface this by saying this movie broke my rating system. If a movie makes me bored at all, it gets a lower score. It gets lowered by actual film flaws too but mostly, the more bored I am the lower score it gets. This is the longest movie I have ever watched by about a half hour and the longest I have ever watched in one sitting (i did take a couple breaks) by about 1hr 20 mins. I was certainly bored for a lot of this but yet I still can't bring myself to lower the score at all. I've heard people say the title is a joke about how this movie isn't happy. I disagree. Not that it is happy, but because this movie is about what it means to be happy. The societal norms and more negative emotions we have to overcome to be happy. If you truly aren't happy in a marriage, why should you feel bad for wanting to leave? If you love a girl and have sex with her, why should you be scolded for that? If you want to be loved, why should you be scared about putting yourself out there? Hamaguchi asks these questions and more in this film. What I will say is the longer the scene, the better in this film, This is the first thing I've watched from him but I've never seen a director use silence more effectively, Going with no score except for scenes where characters are walking or in a vehicle was one of the best choices in any movie. I wasn't even reading subtitles for the book reading yet I was immersed and captivated, especially during the subsequent Q&A. i knew what i was getting into with a 5+ hour movie, but this never felt particularly long. i enjoyed every minute of watching this in the theater, and found myself smiling at random points throughout. if anything i wanted a little more when it ended. the runtime can be intimidating, but the reason for the runtime is that we get some of the best character development and exploration that i’ve ever seen. this is ryusuke hamaguchi in his purest form. 5+ hours of deep, stimulating and often uncomfortable conversation. i’ve said it about both drive my car and wheel of fortune and fantasy; there’s multiple scenes in this film where dialogue lasts for 10+ minutes and i was glued to the screen the whole time. his ability to portray the mundaneness of daily life in such vivid and relatable detail is second to none. at the core of this film is a discussion about what it means to be heard and seen. in one way or another, all four women in this film are at a stage in their life where they feel that the efforts they make go unacknowledged, whether it’s in their romantic life, their professional life, or their personal life. all four women are in positions where they don’t feel seen or heard, and the moments that they spend together are often the only moments they feel like they’re actually being listened to. and true to real relationships, their vulnerability is often not met with unanimous approval and support. the women struggle throughout the film with finding the balance between putting themselves first and devoting their lives to others, whether it be their friends or their significant others. hamaguchi addresses infidelity to a great extent in his films, but i think happy hour is his most human exploration of relationships. the runtime really allows us to be fully immersed in the relationships and decision making of the four women, exposing both the values and the flaws in judgement of each character. i was especially a fan of the nurse with the cunty bob, and found her discussions about her changing role in healthcare. it’s clear that she feels the need to control every aspect of her friends’ lives, or at the very least give her advice and judgements, as this is her role every day at work. her life centers around doing everything for others, to the point where she feels betrayed when jun doesn’t let her in on her relationship troubles. at the end of the movie we see her finally attempt to live for herself and be a little adventurous, which is why she takes Ukai up on his offer to ditch the event with him. this film was an incredibly gripping portrayal of what it’s like living with constant uncertainty. one of the greatest character explorations i’ve ever seen.

I am speechless. It has no right to be this good. Whether it’s the mundane details of everyday life or the most outlandish drama events, Hamaguchi was always able to convert them to pure cinematic wonders. Every second is brimming with possibilities and surprises. The camera is in constant dialogue with its subject, and their roiling emotions beneath the surface. A simple pause or moment of silence could stir up a thousand storms. The workshop scene was a portal (or an invitation) into the film, the words worked as charms in a deceptively soothing rhythm, the gaze and movement held a less explicable yet more captivating power. We went in skeptical but eventually fell under its spell. After Jun left we got the reading event scene, where pretty much every existing order and mechanism was torn down and built anew. Communication became ineffective, and we were forced to stare into a mist, or at a blank paper. The order of everyday life started to collapse through the tiniest cracks, and ended on the lingering gaze and pause of the final scene. Was it hope? Was it confusion? Was it defeat and acceptance?

Con immenso orgoglio posso dire di aver visto 5 ore e 18 minuti di puro cinema indipendente senza mai staccare. Ed infatti è là caratterista principale del capolavoro di Hamaguchi, un film che si fa sempre più denso man mano che si sviluppa. La storia tratta di quattro donne di mezz’età alle prese con la loro routine quotidiana quando una delle quattro decide di divorziare iniziano una serie di eventi che portano a lunghe riflessioni e scontri tra loro ed altri personaggi del film. Le informazioni sui personaggi vengono dati subito circa nei primi 40 minuti e con un escamotage molto curioso e mai visto prima d’ora. Al centro troviamo le discussioni come detto, Hamaguchi vuole parlare e raccontare le donne giapponesi e di come spesso la loro società le costringe a sottomettersi a certi tipi di canoni. Ci mostra queste donne che agli occhi di alcuni personaggi sembrano stiano disobbedendo a determinate regole culturali quando in realtà vogliono solo ritagliarsi un loro spazio dove possono esprimersi e fare come vogliono loro. Il rischio di fare di testa loro, come vogliono loro li porta poi ad un progresso distanziamento da certi tipi di personaggi. Tuttavia il regista persiste e fa in modo che le sue protagoniste non si abbattano e tornino nei canoni richiesti, anzi continuano con la loro battaglia. Ma non tratta solo di questo, proprio le loro azioni o di altri personaggi sono oggetti di dibattito tra loro e dunque un film sulla discussione continua, sul voler cercare un dibattito ed attraverso quello parlare di loro stessi, ed ecco come si scopre qualcosa di nuovo su di loro, sempre di più. Le loro interpretazioni sono incredibili e ti lasciano trasportare fino alla fine del film, quando crediamo di sapere tutto ecco che arriva qualcosa di nuovo. Una loro scelta può cambiare il flusso della storia, dei rapporti ed il riscontro che ne danno altri personaggi mette in dubbio anche il punto di vista dello spettatore. La regia poi lì segue senza sosta li anticipa in ogni azione e sembra quasi li voglia difendere quando devono confrontarsi con altri, difensiva all’esterno e quasi orgogliosa di vedere le quattro amiche insieme, in quel momento l’inquadratura si fa più ampia e lascia respirare le attrici, lasciandole ridere e scherzare, resta così anche nei momenti seri lasciandole discutere animosamente tra loro. Insomma varia in base alla situazione. Nel suo totale un film che rapisce, stanca è vero in certi momenti non nego di aver sentito le 5 ore, ma Hamaguchi ha un modo di raccontare questa storia talmente coinvolgente da perdonargli la durata anzi esserne grato per il tempo dato. A fine film si rimane quasi tristi della sua fine come a voler sapere sempre di più delle loro vite, delle loro battaglie e come i loro rapporti si potrebbero ulteriormente sviluppare.

Not entirely a grieving for 2011, but just about as despairing as any reflection on it from the floating wreckage left behind three or four years on. Immense and so intimate in every shot and detail of that immensity that you really do wind up feeling your brain ooze out of your ears a little bit by the thirdish hour mark. The clinking drinks, beer mugs and wine glasses just making the plastic cup of water stick out. The weak and unconfident smiles in group photos left as the last good memory in ages. Realizations and crunching character revelations unfocused in frame, barely noticeable in sight and script. The ten-years-or-so prequel to a goddamn killer The Golden Girls reboot cast in the obvious and imitable shades of the era’s Kore-eda, but… the Kiyoshi Kurosawa shadows, the silhouettes and faces blurring in jet black against white sunlight… ugh. Jun vanishing into the scarlet of the bus tunnel, Sakurako’s newfound relationship with her mother-in-law and son, Akari hugging her trainee, Fumi dropping like a bag of bricks. And then Jun’s husband revealing his soft and bruised heart. Akari’s hurt feelings and grudges, Fumi’s jealousy. Sakurako’s husband bursting into tears. Upheavals and unplanned disasters and mental breakdowns and ruinings, all stalking and swimming in the seas of day-to-day-like sharks. No one screams, no one yells. The life-defining moments between you and your best friends, the outings and lunches and aimless wanderings that heal, side-by-side with the personal cataclysms that bring to question why the hell anyone goes outside in the first place. It’s all so fragile and poised to collapse, the glass sculpture of poisoned homes and failing marriages. It’s all so much deeper than the cold husbands and unloving fathers and the girls’ day trips that act as sanctuary from them. And drifting over it all like the white clouds of the sunny days, 2011’s nightmare… the Tōhoku earthquake and Fukushima disaster as an End of the World that was simply not allowed to be (gotta go to work, gotta pay the bills, gotta get the groceries, gotta send the kids to school), a fracturing the whole nation limped away from the next morning. Like you could just talk about this one for hours. I think I’m glad overall that Ryusuke seemed to get any and all Yi Yi mimicry out of his system as he got older, but seeing how much of his Thing™️ into the 2020s is clearly rooted in Edward Yangisms stretched so thin as to be the piano wire tapped between the pointed silences is pretty eye-opening. A nice “oh, aHA” click. He might just straight up be Japan’s greatest current filmmaker.
