this film feels like an album from Rachel's This film is, on the one hand, a direct genealogical descendant of the Japanese home drama, a form whose founding grammar runs from Ozu through Kore-eda, and whose central promise, spoken by Shukichi Somiya to his daughter at the end of Late Spring, is that "happiness comes only through effort," that marriage is the first and necessary step toward a shared life. On the other hand, the film is resonates with the psychological intensity and existential desolation of Ingmar Bergman's explorations of marriage, its treatment of incommunicability an translation of Bergman's silence of God into the silence between individuals. Hamaguchi is, like Chantal Akerman, a synthesized fold: Ozu's genre heir and Bergman's structural sibling. This is the condition the nihilistic cinematic unfolding of subjectivity has located only in Chantal Akerman, a filmmaker read as bridging the formal austerity of Yasujiro Ozu and the psychological affective dread of Ingmar Bergman through the female body, so that Ozu's mu and Bergman's void of the soul meet in the feminine gest. Akerman's synthesis is exogenous, it is that of an avant-garde modernist standing outside both traditions, welding them together from a position of formal rupture, the static cage-frame, the durational long take, the refusal of suture. Hamaguchi's synthesis is endogenous, it is that which is working from inside the genre Ozu invented, using its own vocabulary of the home, the teapot, the train platform, the elderly relative's speech about marriage, to arrive at something that behaves, formally and affectively, like Bergman. Where Akerman folds Ozu and Bergman by standing outside both, Hamaguchi folds them by remaining loyal to one while being haunted by the other. Its opening minutes place four women on a train climbing into cloud-covered mountains, an image whose lineage runs directly back to Ozu's own use of train journeys to mark the threshold of marriage, except that where Ozu's journeys carry a young Noriko toward an implied and hopeful five, ten, fifteen years, Hamaguchi's protagonists are already fifteen years past that point, and the line delivered on the mountain, "this resembles our future", inverts the earlier optimism into an admission of unclear, unstable prospects, as Afra Nariman writes in their thesis The Disintegration of Marriage in Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (2015). The red teapot, one of Ozu's most legible motifs of domestic constancy, reappears twice in here, once boiling in the background as Akari receives news of her ex-husband's remarriage and an invitation to Jun's divorce hearing, and once as the sound of its boiling bleeds into an assault scene and then into the shaky-camera ferry departure that closes the film's central act. Paul Schrader's transcendental-style reading treats Ozu's still lifes and codas as reaffirmations that let a character transcend conflict into a kind of static peace. Hasumi Shigehiko's counter-reading, endorsed throughout the nihilistic cinematic unfolding of subjectivity's Ozu fold, insists instead that Ozu's nothingness is material and architectural rather than religious, a tangible nothingness materialized through emptied spaces, and that Ozu himself is, beneath the surface serenity, an extremely cruel director. On this reading, the disintegration the film stages was, in Ozu, held in check by a camera that refused to move. Hamaguchi's innovation is not to invert Ozu's iconography but to give that latent cruelty a body, where Ozu's camera is steady, unwavering, tatami-level, admitting no dollies or zooms, Hamaguchi's shakes precisely at the moments of separation, the car pulling away from Jun at the bus station, the ferry pulling away from the dock, so that the instability Hasumi already located inside Ozu's stillness becomes, in Hamaguchi, kinetic and visible. The film's deepest structural debt to Ozu is temporal. Ozu's mu is bound up with a self-overcoming of nihilism achieved through repetition, the aging gags through which Ozu treats the same plots again and again as a way to slough off nihilism and find a higher health in the ironic, repetitive, banal gestures. This is the vocabulary that Ukai, the workshop leader in the seminar scene, uses, addressing the women after a bodily unconventional communication exercise: "you have to listen to your body again... then you can reconnect... it collapses again. I think it's a repetition of that cycle." Where Ozu leaves this cyclicality entirely implicit in mise-en-scène, the pillow shot as an unchanging form that houses cyclical change, Hamaguchi has a character say it out loud. This is the clearest instance of the film translating Ozu's silent architecture into spoken theory, and it is not an accident that the same logic underwrites the film's setting, as Kobe is a city built on the memory of a catastrophic earthquake. Marriage disintegrates permanently, but the mu-logic of the film insists that something else, such as selfhood, friendship, the capacity to begin again, doesn't disintegrate with it. If Ozu supplies the film's architecture, Bergman supplies its wound. The nihilistic cinematic unfolding of subjectivity's Bergman fold is organized around the close-up as the site where a face is pushed toward regions where socialization and individuation collapse, where two people can occupy the same frame and still be ontologically separated, the paradigm case being Autumn Sonata's confrontation between Charlotte and Eva, as it is the strained shot ever in the history of the close-up. This film stages the identical problem, two people sharing a frame while remaining absolutely unreachable to one another, but solves it by inverse formal means. In the film's divorce-court sequence, Jun and her husband Kohei repeatedly share the same wide shot, but one of them is consistently thrown out of focus while the other remains sharp. Bergman isolates a face in extreme close-up to strip it of social legibility, meanwhile Hamaguchi keeps the two-shot intact and denies optical coherence to one figure inside it. Promixity does not imply communication, and the camera's job is to visualize that gap rather than narrate it. Jun's own words in that scene, that she was killed by her husband not through violence but because he trashed everything she gave him, could be transposed without alteration into Bergman's vocabulary of psychological rather than physical violence, which organizes Scenes from a Marriage, Cries and Whispers, and Autumn Sonata and so many others. Sakurako's marriage supplies the fold's second Bergman-esque register. What the fold calls absolute cold, the affectless, dead-language quality that Bergman's husbands and fathers exhibit across the silence of God cycle. Sakurako's husband tells Jun, from the driver's seat of his car, that he is not the most romantic but that he works and she runs the home, and that works for them, a flat, procedural account of intimacy that carries no more warmth than Kohei's own claim, to Jun's three friends, that marriage binds one to follow a set of rules. Both men speak marriage as arrangement rather than relation, the dead language in Bergman's account of a marriage that has ceased to be lived and become merely administered (Scenes From A Marriage). And this film borrows one further Bergman device wholesale, namely the distribution of a single problematic across an ensemble of women rather than its concentration in one protagonist. Cries and Whispers is a case study of affective problem-Ideas with four powerful lead actresses, problematizing their problematic relation to a shared crisis, the same happens here with marriage itself, its four women, Jun, Sakurako, Fumi, Akari, occupying discrete phases of the institution's collapse: divorced, divorcing, still married and unravelling, and betrayed mid-partnership. Both works share a durational method. Bergman uses the television miniseries format to strip down the film-form to its bare technical necessities, and focus on the relations between Johan and Marianne, Hamaguchi uses 317 minutes to achieve something similar. Both share a vocabulary for what marriage becomes under pressure. Bergman's miniseries tracks a marriage that is mechanically innocent, panics, brushes important concerns off, is terminated, disintegrated, mashed, and rekindled with a few patches, a sequence of verbs that could be redistributed almost intact across Jun, Sakurako, Fumi, and Akari. The decisive divergence is in the destination of the return. Bergman's title already tells us where the disintegration is heading, back into scenes from a marriage, back into the same two-person chamber, famously ending with Johan and Marianne meeting again in the middle of the night, without much fanfare, in a dark house somewhere in the world, an ambiguous, unresolved, but structurally circular rekindling. Jun, Sakurako, Fumi, and Akari do not return to their marriages. Jun does not go back to Kohei, but runs, pregnant, toward an ending the film refuses to resolve. Akari, already divorced for the film's duration, drifts not back toward remarriage-as-repair but sideways, into an unhurried, unpressured relationship with a single father. This is the point at which Ozu's cyclicality and Bergman's dyadic intimacy stop being compatible without adjustment, and it is also the point at which Hamaguchi's fold reveals its own logic, namely, the film needs Bergman's vocabulary of incommunicability to diagnose what is wrong with these marriages, but it needs Ozu's mu-cyclicality, redirected away from the couple and onto the self, to say what happens next. Bergman's dyad, taken on its own, would predict a return to the wound, while Ozu's cyclicality, taken on its own and left in its traditional home-drama form, would predict a return to marriage as cruelty-institution. If one scene in the film functions as the site where the two folds are visibly, formally crossed, it is the unconventional communication seminar. Formally, the scene is Ozu-inflected, de-dramatized, basically plotless, composed of mundane, repeated, almost ritual gestures, foreheads pressed together, ears against bellies, the kind of nothing happens duration associated with mu's architecture of banality. And yet the content of what is said inside that duration is thoroughly Bergman in its ambitions, as it is a seminar of an attempt to reach, through the body, a form of contact that ordinary social and verbal communication under patriarchy has foreclosed, the project Bergman's close-up performs through the face when he pushes it to the point where the individual, socialization, and communication collapse. Ukai's language of losing and needing to relocate one's center mass is the film's statement of the cyclical mu-logic ("it collapses again... a repetition of that cycle") delivered inside a scene whose entire premise is Bergman's problem: how do two bodies, in the same room, actually reach one another? The workshop is thus the film's structural keystone because it is where Ozu's silent formal cyclicality is translated into speech, and where Bergman's crisis of intimacy is translated into an ordinary, almost banal, group exercise rather than a private confession between two people in extremis. The film's critical apparatus organizes its account of character around a single recurring formulation: "Am I who I want to be?" The women's lives are structured as "theatre," a set of imposed roles, nurse, housewife, divorcée, that must be broken through via discursive decorum in order to reach "moments of genuine emotional honesty. Sakurako must ask her husband's permission before making plans with friends, Jun requires her husband's cooperation to be granted a divorce at all, her body's future partially controlled by koseki-era family law that permits a husband to claim a child that is not biologically his, Fumi's autonomy as a career woman becomes, in her husband's eyes, a threat serious enough to justify seeking out someone more dependent. In each case a script, whether domestic, legal, or marital, stands between the woman and a truer, more honest self. This is now where we will turn to stress-test a theory of the self against the film, because "Am I who I want to be?" is the question at the center of Pete Wolfendale's account of personal identity in The Revenge of Reason. In "Beyond Survival," Wolfendale defines the self neither as the body that makes action possible nor as a fixed goal that dictates every choice in advance, but as the locus of that fundamental question, he asks it in exactly these words: "Who do I want to be?". So let's see: does Hamaguchi's film, when its central question is read through Wolfendale's actual theory of selfhood, hold up, or does it reveal exactly where a rationalist, anti-essentialist account of personhood parts ways with a film that keeps reaching, visually and thematically, for the body as the site of truth? Wolfendale's account of the self, developed across "Beyond Survival" and "On Containing Multitudes," is built to exclude the picture it might seem to license at first glance, that of a hidden, authentic interior self that social roles conceal and that honest self-expression recovers. He defines a person formally as a system whose behaviour is driven by the divergence between two representations, one of how the world is and one of how it should be, and he insists this makes the self neither simply the physical platform nor an overarching goal that prescribes each action in all its details but the standing, unresolved question itself. Selfhood on this account is achieved and ongoing rather than given and static, personal identity is not a substance persisting beneath change but something closer to a plan continually revised in light of what actually happens, its content read back into the original intention only after the fact, as if this is what was truly intended all along. Most importantly, Wolfendale diagnoses and rejects the picture the language of "true self" invites. Discussing the theatrical vocabulary of role and mask directly, he notes that it invites us to imagine the true person beneath these masks and warns that this is exactly the wrong move, because there is no pre-existent unified self of the kind the mask-metaphor presupposes. And autonomy, for Wolfendale, is not liberation from all determination into some unconditioned freedom, but the capacity to bring one's priorities into question, and to revise them, a holistic revision of practical commitments in which all evolve together and none is beyond reform. Read this way, the film's ending, that the women's truth is found not in the preservation of social scripts, but in the courage to live on after those scripts have failed, survives the stress test rather well, provided the phrase "true self" in its critical apparatus is quietly corrected. What actually happens to Jun, Sakurako, and Akari is not the unveiling of a self that was always there under the housewife or divorcée costume, but a wholesale, effortful revision of commitments, undertaken without any guarantee of a settled destination. Jun's flight is, in Wolfendale's terms, the revisionary vector implicit in every process of self-construction being allowed, for once, to operate without limit, a self choosing to redefine itself rather than defaulting to the preservation of an existing arrangement, which is precisely the fork in the road Wolfendale poses at the close of "Beyond Survival": do we default to survival as a fundamental drive, or do we take the challenge to our self-interest as an opportunity to explicitly redefine ourselves? Akari's slow, unpressured relationship with the single father reads as self-realisation, as the achievement of those ends that we choose for ourselves, which may include but is never obligated to prioritize the survival of a prior social form. And the film's refusal to stage a return to the marriage-form itself, unlike Bergman's Johan and Marianne, is what Wolfendale would predict of genuinely autonomous agents. Marriage here is treated as one commitment among others rather than the autopoietic circle whose survival is assumed to be the point, the same circle Wolfendale insists a genuinely free self must be capable of unravelling. Wolfendale is a committed critic of what he calls "the embodiment paradigm", the tendency, inherited from certain strands of phenomenology and affect theory, to treat lived experience and bodily immediacy as a more authentic register of selfhood than explicit, revisable, discursive commitment, and to substitute the capacity to suffer, or in this case, the capacity to touch and be touched, for autonomy as the source of moral worth. Ukai's workshop stages this substitution, as its premise is that verbal, socially-coded communication has failed the four women, and that something more honest can be reached by returning to the body, losing and relocating one's center mass, listening to the body again as though it holds a truth that words have covered over. This is close to what Wolfendale, closing "Artificial Bodies and the Promise of Abstraction," calls somatic chauvinism that cannot imagine forms of life that look nothing like its own, which is the assumption that immediacy is not only the content of authentic selfhood but its necessary form. If the film simply endorsed Ukai's premise, it would be reaching, at its structural center, for the account of the given self that Wolfendale's rationalism criticizes. But the film is more guarded here, and this is where the stress test produces something more interesting than either confirmation or refutation. Nariman's thesis says that Ukai's status is deliberately left unresolved, "it is left unclear whether he is something like a con-artist, or a genuine figure in the film", and the film stages his speech with a wandering, untethered camera that breaks from Ozu's discipline without settling into Bergman's intimacy either, simply drifts. The women who most need what he is offering, Sakurako above all,  leave the workshop moved but not delivered, her marriage does not improve, her husband's coldness does not dissolve under the pressure of a rediscovered center. What the scene actually demonstrates is closer to Wolfendale, that the somatic exercise is a stimulus for revision, not a substitute for it, changing what the women are willing to question, not what they essentially already are. In this way, the workshop scene is the film staging the temptation of that position and declining to resolve it, which puts the film, at its most ambiguous moment, closer to Wolfendale's rationalism than a first pass at the scene would suggest. Furthermore, Wolfendale's essay on selfhood also develops an account of "personae", which are defined as relatively stable configurations of behaviour that can go dormant and be reactivated, requiring only enough coherence across switches to remain a single locus of authority and responsibility, without requiring a hidden unifying depth. It is worth asking more speculatively, whether the films's four-woman ensemble should be read not only as four separate Wolfendalean selves each revising her own commitments in parallel, the reading we've mostly assumed, but as something closer to a single distributed subject-position within the patriarchal script, refracted across four bodies the way Nariman's own phases (divorced, divorcing, married-and-disintegrating, betrayed career woman) imply a shared underlying problematic rather than four unrelated case studies. Wolfendale's own criteria for genuine plurality are demanding, namely differentiated authority and responsibility, and the real possibility of conflict between the loci in question, and the four women do sometimes disagree sharply about how to interpret Jun's disappearance, which is at least a plausible instance of exactly this criterion being met. This reading cannot be settled on the film's own terms, but it is the kind of extension a genuine stress test should surface. What survives the stress test, in the end, is thus that Wolfendale's insistence that the wrong done to Sakurako and Jun is not that their roles conceal their real selves, but that those roles were undertaken and sustained without the possibility of revision, Sakurako required her husband's permission for something as small as a weekend trip, while Jun required her husband's cooperation merely to end the marriage. What is violated in each case is the standing that Wolfendale identifies with personhood itself, namely the unique authority a self must retain over the force, though not the entire content, of its own commitments. The koseki system, and the husbands who invoke it as the rules a wife must live by, are not concealing Sakurako's and Jun's true selves, but are denying them of the thing Wolfendale's theory makes constitutive of selfhood as such, which is the ongoing right to ask, and to keep asking, who do I want to be.

I was curious, since I hadn't watched this film in a few years, whether it still held up as my favorite, and I can safely say it does. Similar to what I appreciated about it upon my first viewing, the points of conflict never lean towards one party; they simply reveal how two different well-meaning people can arrive at two different conclusions based on their own personalities and past experiences. This approach to the film's screenwriting makes for a realistic portrayal of adult-age conflict between long-time friends. Also, for a film filled with mostly lengthy scenes with little more than dialogue, it keeps you on your feet during its 5-hour runtime. I felt like I was a fly on the wall, watching these dynamics between the four friends, the people in their individual lives, and the people they meet along the way unfold. I was also surprised to learn that these were mostly first-time actors! Every one of the lead actors brought such a convincing and distinct portrayal of their character that I never would have known. Personally, Akari's hard shell and her approach to trust spoke to me. As someone whose past experiences have made me reluctant to open up or trust others easily, her character arc toward becoming more vulnerable was a highlight. Besides the captivating dialogue and plot, this was shot beautifully. From the opening scene revealing the four main characters to the shots of Kusatsu to the nightclub scene, there were multiple times when I took out my phone to capture a shot that blew me away. Hamaguchi's films have a consistent pattern of slow-burn, in-depth examinations of subjects, and this feels like the quintessential example of that. I want to keep revisiting this every few years as I grow closer to the characters' ages to see how I further relate to them in different ways <3

我心中最理想的配置，會是《在車上》跟《歡樂時光》交錯著看。這禮拜看《歡樂時光》，下禮拜看《在車上》，如果能一直反覆反覆著看就太好了。 五個半小時的《歡樂時光》，它不能切成五份，它不可能也不可以拍成影集，它是最特殊的觀影體驗。 從一開始的那個鏡頭，我們跟著女主角們坐在火車裡，搖搖晃晃的穿過綠色隧道。我們會發現，《歡樂時光》提供的不只是一個故事，它還邀請你一起跟主角們旅行、野餐、參加工作坊與朗讀會。我們不只是旁觀一個故事，還彷彿置身其中，跟著主角們一起煩惱，跟著主角們一起焦慮。 ★ 我讀了這部電影的電影書《在鏡頭前表演》，裡面提到，電影中的工作坊只跟表演者決議了流程，就用拍紀錄片的方式拍出來，但第一次沒有拍到需要的素材，大約兩個月之後再拍了一次。 這一段事實上沒有劇情，但我們的情緒被工作坊本身牽引，這兩個人背靠背能不能順利的站起來？四個人呢？全部人一起呢？這次會成功嗎？ 而整個後編都在呼應著前編工作坊的「倚靠」主題，四個女主角有時候互相倚靠，有時候摔倒，但大多數都能接住對方——即使沒有出現，也沒有真的缺席。 電影快結束時，向來很兇的明里給學妹一個擁抱，很深很深，很久很久。這部電影就是這樣，看完像是被擁抱了一樣，而且不是輕率的擁抱，是貫串過去現在未來的擁抱。 ★ 那到底什麼是「歡樂時光」？ 前編的工作坊結束時，帶領的鵜飼說： 「背對背站立、聆聽五臟六腑、貼額頭⋯⋯我不知道這些事有沒有意義。但平常我們不太有機會嘗試這些溝通方式。」 「如果人我之間能建立完美的平衡，那或許會是很幸福的一段時光。但我們也會不斷的在關係中失重，不斷的需要找回這種感覺。」 「希望大家把在工作坊學會的東西，帶回日常生活中。」

《歡樂時光》 因為《在車上》開始認識 濱口竜介 這位導演，從《偶然與想像》看見精巧的「對話」如何塑造電影的靈動感，但真正讓我愛上濱口電影的，則是《歡樂時光》。 《歡樂時光》講述四位友好女性的日常，劇情圍繞在看似平凡無奇的生活中，各自所面臨的情感困境。 《歡樂時光》的主題是「溝通」，也是濱口電影的主旋律。雖然有人認為濱口大量使用對話來推進劇情的電影風格，有點「話癆」。但這次在電影院欣賞《歡樂時光》，則讓我更加確定，濱口的電影不只是在對話上有獨到的設計外，同時鏡頭語言的掌握也很厲害。 電影好幾幕的對話，鏡頭都是正對著說話者，使觀眾彷彿在角色面前「聆聽」其講述。然後在多人交談的場景時，透過適當的剪輯調度，讓交叉紛雜的對話鮮活而不單調，且情緒轉折與氛圍改變時也很自然。 電影中除了可看到濱口擅長的「車內對話」外，在電車和某些移動場景，更可見其善於運用自然的光影明暗，來傳達角色幽微的心境變化。 而《歡樂時光》最吸引我的，還是在於演員們在鏡頭前真誠地袒露自我，表達那些生活中被壓抑已久的心聲，呈現了「語言」、「非語言」的溝通，以及溝通的「阻礙」與「抵達」，還有那試圖觸及他人內心的「意願」。
